clue.text: Comelier liar, perhaps, as romantic novelist

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the two words could be something else, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A more comely liar is offered as a fitting description of a writer of romances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange COMELIER LIAR; the twelve letters spell the Victorian best-selling romantic novelist's pen name.
explanation.definitionFit: She was a hugely popular Victorian author of melodramatic romances such as A Romance of Two Worlds.

clue.text: Poet seen to wonder at student

parts.note: to wonder at something is to marvel
L is the learner plate abbreviation for a student or learner driver

explanation.surface: A poet is observed gazing in amazement at a pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Marvell was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical poet, author of To His Coy Mistress.

clue.text: Right Arab state in French novel

parts.note: Oman is a sultanate in the Arabian peninsula

explanation.surface: A right-wing Gulf state appears as a setting in a French book.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a novel is roman, as in roman à clef.

clue.text: He foresaw the fall of Paris long before this year's eclipse watchers

definitions.text: He foresaw the fall of Paris long before this year's eclipse watchers

parts.words: He foresaw the fall of Paris long before this year's eclipse watchers
parts.note: points to the Soviet writer whose novel The Fall of Paris was written in 1941, long before the eclipse watchers of the year of publication

explanation.surface: A prophet predicted the collapse of Paris well ahead of the crowds watching this year's eclipse.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'fall of Paris' is the title of the Russian writer Ilya Ehrenburg's 1941 novel, so 'foresaw' plays on writing it rather than predicting history.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilya Ehrenburg, Soviet journalist and novelist, wrote The Fall of Paris, which won a Stalin Prize.

clue.text: Has start of old Waugh novel, supposedly

indicators.note: start of is read as applying to each of the following words, taking the opening letter of every one

explanation.surface: Someone possesses the beginning of an early Evelyn Waugh book, or so it is claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of' looks as if it applies to 'old' alone, but it takes the first letter of all four words: old, Waugh, novel, supposedly.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess something is to hold it as one's own property.

clue.text: Part of stage entertainment, roughly at centre

indicators.note: roughly suggests the letters of the following two words are only approximately in order

explanation.surface: A section of a theatrical show takes place roughly in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges AT CENTRE; the result is the French term for an interval piece in a play or opera.
explanation.definitionFit: An interlude performed between the acts of a play or opera is a portion of the whole show.

clue.text: Lean over, we hear, for piano virtuoso ()

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for leaning over is spoken, giving a name of the same sound

parts.note: a ship that leans over is said to list

explanation.surface: A great pianist bends forward at the keyboard, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: A list is a tilt to one side; said out loud it matches the surname of the Hungarian composer and pianist Franz Liszt.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the most celebrated keyboard showman of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: French poet takes on fuel, much used by the Impressionists

parts.note: René Char was a twentieth-century French poet
coal is a fuel burnt in fires and furnaces

explanation.surface: A French poet stocks up on fuel, popular with Impressionist painters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes on' simply joins the poet to the fuel. The definition is the drawing material sketched with by artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Sticks of burnt wood make a soft black drawing medium that many nineteenth-century painters sketched with.

clue.text: Is this a dagger that I see before me? (see note)

definitions.text: Is this a dagger that I see before me?

parts.words: Is this a dagger that I see before me?
parts.note: Macbeth's line is borrowed to describe the printer's dagger mark, a typographical symbol

explanation.surface: Macbeth's famous question about a vision of a dagger.
explanation.walkthrough: The dagger here is not a weapon but the printer's dagger sign used to mark a footnote or a doubtful passage.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name for the dagger-shaped mark used in printing to point to a note or flag a spurious passage.

clue.text: Night watchman?

parts.note: read not as a guard but as the man who painted The Night Watch, a Dutch group portrait

explanation.surface: A security guard on the late shift.
explanation.walkthrough: A night watchman is a guard, but here it is the painter of The Night Watch, the famous Amsterdam group portrait of a militia company.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch master painted the celebrated militia portrait known as The Night Watch in 1642.

clue.text: A European in Forster's India was a "hibernating animal", to some extent ()

indicators.note: to some extent says only part of the quoted words is wanted, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: In A Passage to India, a European was likened to a hibernating creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'waS A HIBernating'. The definition is the title Indians gave a European man in British India, as in E M Forster's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: In colonial India a white European man was addressed by this respectful title meaning master.

clue.text: Disruptive South American influence resulting in one-nil

indicators.note: disruptive implies the letters of the scoreline are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A troublesome South American force leads to a one-nil result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disruptive' reads as part of the definition, but it rearranges ONE-NIL; 'resulting in' just links it.
explanation.definitionFit: The periodic warming of the Pacific off Peru affects weather patterns worldwide.

clue.text: History spoken in symphony

parts.note: history is what is in the past
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: Historical events are recounted out loud within a symphonic work.
explanation.walkthrough: The symphony meant is Beethoven's Sixth, nicknamed the Pastoral.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Sixth Symphony is known by this name for its depiction of country life.

clue.text: One of those associated with Hercules

definitions.text: One of those associated with Hercules

parts.words: One of those associated with Hercules
parts.note: Hercules is famous for twelve tasks set by King Eurystheus, and this is one of them

explanation.surface: Someone linked with the mythical strongman Hercules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those associated with' suggests followers or companions, but the reference is to the twelve tasks of Hercules; the word is also a British political party, which adds to the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the twelve heroic tasks set for Hercules is called by this word, meaning hard work.

clue.text: Prohibit Bordeaux, for example, to French poet

parts.note: to prohibit is to ban
Bordeaux is an example of a French town, ville in French

explanation.surface: A ban on Bordeaux wine is proposed to a poet in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Bordeaux looks like the wine, but it is the city, and 'ville' is French for town.
explanation.definitionFit: Théodore de Banville was a nineteenth-century French Parnassian poet.

clue.text: Those who bless the squire, should always know their proper ones, Dickens wrote

definitions.text: Those who bless the squire, should always know their proper ones, Dickens wrote

parts.words: Those who bless the squire, should always know their proper ones, Dickens wrote
parts.note: recalls the rhyme in The Chimes about blessing the squire and his relations and knowing one's proper social place

explanation.surface: Dickens wrote that the poor who bless the squire should keep to their place.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Chimes, Dickens mocks the rhyme: 'O let us love our occupations, Bless the squire and his relations... And always know our proper' places in society.
explanation.definitionFit: One's position in the social order is a rank or standing, and the rhyme ends on this word.

clue.text: David Benedictus wrote of this century man

definitions.text: David Benedictus wrote of this century man

parts.words: David Benedictus wrote of this century man
parts.note: points to the ordinal century in the title of a work by the English novelist David Benedictus

explanation.surface: A novelist wrote about the man of the present century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this century' reads as 'our own century'; the clue asks for the word that names that century.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1900s are the ordinal century following the nineteenth, the setting of the book's title.

clue.text: Some of Patrick Leigh Fermor's "divine maquisards", like Chiron

definitions.text: Some of Patrick Leigh Fermor's "divine maquisards", like Chiron

parts.words: Some of Patrick Leigh Fermor's "divine maquisards", like Chiron
parts.note: the travel writer called the mythical half-horse creatures of the Greek hills divine resistance fighters, and Chiron was the wisest of them

explanation.surface: Patrick Leigh Fermor's godlike Greek guerrillas included someone like Chiron.
explanation.walkthrough: Patrick Leigh Fermor, who fought with the Cretan resistance, applied the wartime term 'maquisards' (guerrillas) to the half-man, half-horse beings of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiron was the wise half-human, half-horse tutor of Achilles in Greek myth.

clue.text: Wild heron carrying egg for one of The Six

indicators.note: carrying means the bird holds the other word within it
wild suggests the letters of the bird are running out of control into a new order

explanation.surface: An unruly heron flies off with an egg belonging to a group of six.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges the bird to HONER, and 'carrying' puts the egg inside it. Les Six were a group of twentieth-century French composers including Poulenc and Milhaud.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Honegger was a Swiss-born composer, a member of the French group of composers known as Les Six.

clue.text: Walpole or Lofting, we hear, Richard or Ted

indicators.note: we hear signals that the shared first names are spoken to give a surname of the same sound

parts.note: Hugh Walpole and Hugh Lofting were both novelists called Hugh, so two of them are Hughs

explanation.surface: Writers named Walpole or Lofting are mentioned alongside Richard or Ted.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Walpole and Hugh Lofting share the first name, so together they are two Hughs; spoken, that is the surname of the novelist Richard and the poet Ted.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Hughes wrote A High Wind in Jamaica and Ted Hughes was Poet Laureate, so both share the surname.

clue.text: Children were warned by his stories

definitions.text: Children were warned by his stories

parts.words: Children were warned by his stories
parts.note: points to the author of Cautionary Tales for Children, comic verses warning children against bad behaviour

explanation.surface: An author's tales served as warnings to the young.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilaire Belloc's Cautionary Tales for Children (1907) includes Matilda, who told lies and was burned to death.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc wrote the comic verse collection Cautionary Tales for Children.

clue.text: Approximately about a thousandth friend of David Simple

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes around the following words

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means approximately
a mill is a thousandth of a dollar

explanation.surface: Roughly a thousandth part of a companion of a literary hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps circa round the rest. A mill is a US money unit of a tenth of a cent. David Simple is Sarah Fielding's 1744 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Sarah Fielding's novel The Adventures of David Simple, she is one of the true friends the hero finds.

clue.text: Gaunt character from Charles Reade

parts.note: Gaunt is not thin here but the surname of the title figure of a Charles Reade novel, whose first name is wanted

explanation.surface: A thin, haggard figure from a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaunt' looks like an adjective meaning thin, but Griffith Gaunt (1866) is a novel by Charles Reade, and its hero's first name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade's 1866 novel is titled after its hero, Griffith Gaunt.

clue.text: Like Walton's receipts ()

parts.note: Izaak Walton's Compleat Angler includes recipes, old-fashioned receipts, for cooking the catch

explanation.surface: Resembling the receipts of a man called Walton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receipts' is the old word for recipes, and Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler gives recipes for cooking fish; the answer also means suspicious, as receipts might be.
explanation.definitionFit: Recipes from a book on angling are about cooking the catch, and the word also suggests something suspicious.

clue.text: It runs softly and drowns the Past, Edward Thomas thought

definitions.text: It runs softly and drowns the Past, Edward Thomas thought

parts.words: It runs softly and drowns the Past, Edward Thomas thought
parts.note: describes flowing water as pictured in a poem by Edward Thomas, the English poet killed in 1917

explanation.surface: The poet Edward Thomas imagined something running gently and drowning memory.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Thomas's poem pictures flowing water as something that 'runs softly and drowns the Past'; 'runs' is the clue's hint at running water.
explanation.definitionFit: A small river or brook runs gently along its course.

clue.text: … I'll sweat and seek about for -" (Troilus and Cressida) ()

definitions.text: I'll sweat and seek about for -" (Troilus and Cressida)

parts.words: I'll sweat and seek about for -" (Troilus and Cressida)
parts.note: the missing word of Pandarus's closing speech in the Shakespeare play, where he seeks relief from his ailments

explanation.surface: A line from Pandarus's epilogue in Troilus and Cressida with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Pandarus ends the play with 'Till then I'll sweat and seek about for' the word wanted, meaning remedies or comforts for his diseases.
explanation.definitionFit: Reliefs or comforts are what the ailing Pandarus sweats and searches for.

clue.text: Star of Cocteau's Le Be Indifférent Entries submitted from

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Star of Cocteau's Le Be Indifférent Entries submitted from', carries stray page text ('Entries submitted from') and 'Le Be' for 'Le Bel'; no scan to give the printed clue.
annotationWithheld.clue: Star of Cocteau's Le Be Indifférent Entries submitted from

clue.text: Not The Bell, but one of three ()

definitions.text: Not The Bell, but one of three

parts.words: Not The Bell, but one of three
parts.note: sets aside an Iris Murdoch novel; three Victorian sisters shared one pen surname, and the pseudonymous first name of one of them is wanted

explanation.surface: Not the novel The Bell, but one of a trio.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brontës published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell; the Ellis was Emily. The Bell is an Iris Murdoch novel, which the clue sets aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights under the pen name Ellis Bell, one of three sibling pseudonyms.

clue.text: As widespread as Robert Coover's Baseball Association

definitions.meaning: something found everywhere or affecting everyone
Robert Coover's 1968 novel is The ... Baseball Association, Inc., J. Henry Waugh, Prop.

explanation.definitionFit: Something found everywhere is general to all, and Coover's novel names its imaginary dice-game league with this adjective.

clue.text: Those with an ocean view from 1ac?

definitions.text: Those with an ocean view from 1ac?

parts.words: Those with an ocean view from 1ac?
parts.note: points to the title of a work by the romantic novelist at 1 across, read as eyes looking out across the water

explanation.surface: People with a sea view, possibly from the first answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those with an ocean view' are the organs of sight looking seawards; the title is a story by the novelist at 1 across, Marie Corelli.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a tale by the Victorian romantic novelist, and also describes organs of sight gazing across the water.
